h.strategy: Measured interaction effects are dominated by a few robust regularities: an edit's effect is larger when the parent is weak overall and smaller when the parent is already strong (ceiling and floor); a component's removal costs less when another component already fills the same role; and an edit's effect changes most when the conditioning field controls the main bottleneck. Build each hypothesis on one of these, stated as a specific conditional. Prefer conditions that change overall parent quality substantially over conditions with subtle effects. Do not chase counterintuitive sign reversals. Spread hypotheses across different edited and conditioning fields, and use both HIGHER and LOWER directions roughly equally.

hyps.why: Edge 1 feeds node 2, whose only exit is edge 5, so a conv there is wasted when edge 5 is none.
Edge 2's output only reaches node 3 via edge 5, so with edge 5 gone the conv has little effect.
Replacing a removed edge with a strong conv gives a larger gain than replacing a non-trivial op.
Replacing 'none' with a conv restores the node 1 path, a bigger gain than swapping one working op for another.
Replacing 'none' with a conv adds a new path, a bigger gain than replacing an existing op.
Replacing 'none' with a skip restores a path, a larger gain than replacing an existing op.
Adding a skip where the direct edge was removed restores gradient flow, a large gain.
Replacing a strong conv with a pool loses a lot, so the effect is more negative than when replacing a weak op.
Downgrading a strong conv to a skip costs more than changing an already weak op.
Downgrading from a 3x3 conv to 1x1 loses capacity, so the effect is worse than when replacing a weak op.
